title: AI-assisted development of Kkakkak: Blender blanks, procedural pencil cuts, and real recorded tool sounds
author: porche911_kr
selftext:
I'm the developer of Kkakkak, a small Android pencil-whittling game. The attached 18-second clip is a recording of the running app with English UI.

![video](en56fj05phzh1 "Actual Kkakkak gameplay with English UI and recorded tool sounds.")

AI disclosure: AI coding assistance was used for the app implementation, development tools and Blender asset-authoring scripts. AI also assisted with the promotional text. This is a commercial game with free core tools and optional purchases.

The useful development boundary in this project is the difference between an authored asset and the changing workpiece. The Blender library supplies material and tool blanks, meshes and material definitions. Runtime cutting then changes the workpiece surface from those definitions; shrinking a static pencil model would not implement the carving interaction. The test-paper mark is based on the tip's cross-section, so sharpening has a visible consequence beyond the model itself.

The asset pipeline includes geometry checks for finite coordinates, normalized normals, index bounds, zero-area faces and catalog consistency. Those checks are useful gates for AI-assisted code and tooling, but they don't establish that the knife contacts the right point or that the interaction feels good on a phone. Those are separate runtime checks.

The clip's cutting sounds use real recordings of the tools, rather than generated voice or music. The game also lets the player blow shavings away using on-device microphone detection.

The HB pencil and pencil knife are free; extra pencils and tools are one-time purchases. No subscription, ads or account.

Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ootssu.kkakkak

For other developers using coding assistants with procedural geometry: which invariant or visual check has caught the most convincing-looking but incorrect output for you?
